Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01From trajectories to a probability density Suppose x receives stochastic increments Δx in short intervals Δt. Define drift A and diffusion B from the first two increment moments per unit time. This small-increment approximation fails when large jumps dominate. A(x,t)=lim⟨Δx⟩Δt, B(x,t)=lim⟨(Δx)²⟩Δt Let f integrate to one over the full real line. The one-step squared increment defining B is distinct from the total squared displacement since the initial time. 02Expand the evolution through second order Expand the transition-probability evolution in Δx. When higher increment moments can be neglected, the first two terms give the Fokker–Planck equation. Its apparent factor of two depends on the convention used for B. ∂f∂t=−∂(Af)∂x+12∂²(Bf)∂x²=−∂J∂x J=Af−12∂(Bf)∂x Zero boundary flux conserves total probability; an absorbing boundary removes it. Conservation depends on boundary conditions as well as the differential equation. 03A solvable model: restoring drift plus diffusion Choose A = −γx, B = 2D, γ ≥ 0 and D > 0. This Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model combines restoring drift with random excitation. A Gaussian initial distribution remains Gaussian while its mean and variance evolve. d⟨x⟩dt=−γ⟨x⟩, dVdt=−2γV+2D μ(t)=μ₀e−γt V(t)=V₀e−2γt+Dγ(1−e−2γt) (γ>0) Multiply the PDE by x or x² and integrate by parts to derive the moment equations. At γ = 0 the variance is V₀ + 2Dt and keeps growing. 04Animate the distribution and its stationary state f(x,t)=1√(2πV(t))exp[−(x−μ(t))²2V(t)] γ>0 : feq∝exp[−γx²2D] The panel uses dimensionless x,t, D = 0.5, μ₀ = 2 and V₀ = 0.0625. It plots an analytic solution, not self-consistent cluster collision coefficients. Tails outside the window are retained mathematically; the visible area is not renormalized to one. 05Additional ingredients for star clusters Clusters require position–velocity distributions or orbit-averaged energy distributions. Even at fixed potential, phase-space f(E) differs from number per energy N(E) = g(E)f(E); the density of states g(E) matters. Encounter coefficients depend on the stellar distribution and the potential must be updated with Poisson’s equation. An evolving potential also changes energy coordinates. Escape boundaries, binaries and multiple stellar masses can be important. The OU model exchanges energy with a bath and generally does not conserve kinetic energy. It is not a calculation of cooling or gravothermal collapse in an isolated cluster. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For A = −γx and B = 2D, let γ = 2 and D = 0.5. Find the limiting mean and variance. What changes at γ = 0? Show the answer and reasoning Mean tends to zero and variance to D/γ = 0.25, giving standard deviation 0.5. With γ = 0, variance grows as its initial value plus 2Dt; no normalizable stationary Gaussian is reached on the full real line.
